prompt.context: The CEO of Chemicals Inc., a leading chemicals company with a long history of innovative products and application technologies has contacted you for assistance. In the past couple of years, the company's bottom-line profitability has slowly eroded to the point where EBITDA is hovering barely above 0, even though the company's overall sales growth is outpacing industry averages. Magnifying these financial problems are the reports he is receiving from his business unit leaders which are that revenues and volumes are up and profitability has never been higher.
prompt.question: The CEO looks at you across the table and asks: 'What do I do?'

clarifying_info.q: Tell me about the firm's product portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: Many different kinds of chemicals products, sold to many different kinds of customers (large, small), in many different kinds of industries (automotive, medical, consumer products), all around the globe.

The company is organized geographically and by the underlying technologies that drive products, not necessarily by product line. Definition of product line is technology-application (think industry)-geography, e.g. Chemical A – Automotive – USA.

clarifying_info.q: What industries are customers of the firm's products?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive, Medical, Consumer Products (packaging), Manufacturing, Electronics, Drilling.

clarifying_info.q: How does the firm view the world in terms of regions?
clarifying_info.a: North America, South America, Europe, Pacific.

clarifying_info.q: Who are their competitors? What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: Major competitors include large multi-national corporations as well as small, local, specialized firms with a single product. Some of these firms actually purchase our client's products and rework them and sell to the end customer.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs the company is incurring?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues last year were $2Bn. The COGS is variable, about 25%, but all companies in this industry are dealing with fluctuating feedstock prices. SG&A expense is 30% of revenue and beyond the industry benchmark. Other costs are inline with industry norms.

exhibits.title: Product Line Contribution Margins
exhibits.shows: A bar chart displaying contribution margins (in $/kg) for 15 product lines, ranging from 0 to 250 $/kg. Each bar represents a distinct product line. Bars are color-coded by business unit (Technology A, Technology B, Technology C).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: Contribution Margins in $/kg, scale 0–250. 15 bars of varying heights. Three color categories corresponding to Technology A, Technology B, and Technology C.

framework: Identify the disconnect: sales revenues and volumes are up but overall EBITDA is near 0 while BU leaders report record profitability — suggests a cost allocation problem
Focus on cost structure: examine COGS (variable ~25% of revenue) and SG&A (30% of revenue, above industry benchmark) as primary drivers of margin erosion

Analyze the product and service mix: assess whether all 15 product lines across 3 technologies and 5 industries are receiving the same level of service and whether that service cost is appropriately allocated
Examine customer profitability by segment: understand what each customer segment needs, what they are willing to pay, and whether the firm is undercharging for value-added services
Assess organizational structure: company is organized by technology BU, which may misalign cost ownership with the product lines and geographies that generate (or consume) margin
Evaluate commoditization risk: contribution margin data (Exhibit 1) reveals a wide range across the 15 product lines, indicating some products have been commoditized while others remain specialty

questions.prompt: Walk through the cost structure of Chemicals Inc. and identify where the problem likely lies.
questions.guidance: Revenues = $2Bn. COGS ~25% = $500M (variable, feedstock-driven, in line with industry). SG&A = 30% = $600M (above industry benchmark — key red flag). Total costs before other items = 55% of revenue. EBITDA barely above 0 implies total costs consume nearly 100% of revenue. The anomaly is SG&A being above industry norm. Candidate should identify SG&A as the likely source of the problem and probe cost allocation.

math.setup: Revenue = $2,000M; COGS = 25% of revenue; SG&A = 30% of revenue
steps: EBITDA ≈ 0 implies remaining costs (manufacturing overhead, D&A add-backs, etc.) account for near remaining 45%
SG&A at 30% is flagged as above industry benchmark — this is the primary lever to investigate
math.answer: SG&A of $600M (30% of $2Bn revenue) is above industry benchmark and is the primary driver of margin compression. COGS at 25% is in line with the industry.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What insights do you draw from the contribution margin data?
questions.guidance: The 15 product lines span a very wide range of contribution margins (from near 0 to ~250 $/kg). This wide dispersion indicates significant commoditization across much of the portfolio. Business units (Technology A, B, C) are spread across the entire continuum — no single BU owns only high-margin or only low-margin products. Key insight: the firm applies the same full suite of shared services (small batch sizes, custom logistics, technical/customer support, application development) to all 15 product lines regardless of their margin contribution. High-cost services are being provided to low-margin (commodity) products, destroying value. Candidate should suggest realigning product lines based on contribution margin rather than technology.

math.answer: Qualitative insight: wide contribution margin range (approximately 0 to 250 $/kg) across 15 product lines; same service model applied to all regardless of margin — cost misallocation confirmed.

questions.prompt: What changes to product/service model and organization would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose splitting the business into Specialty and Commodity segments based on contribution margin. Specialty (high-margin): continue full-service model — custom logistics, technical support, application development. Commodity (low-margin): adopt a low-cost service model — IT-enabled self-service, a la carte service agreements, less favorable terms. Additionally, a single leader per shared service function should own cost allocation and negotiate service-level agreements with each BU to ensure appropriate resourcing and cost transparency.

math.answer: Organizational restructure; no numeric math required.

questions.prompt: What additional changes might you consider for an organization facing increased commoditization of product lines?
questions.guidance: Possible answers: (1) Invest in R&D to continually innovate and push commodity products up the value chain into specialty; (2) Exit commodity product lines or outsource manufacturing to low-cost producers; (3) Develop industry-specific sales teams that span BUs and focus on high-value customer relationships; (4) Explore strategic partnerships or acquisitions with specialty chemicals players; (5) Consider portfolio pruning — divest commodity BU to focus exclusively on specialty.

math.answer: Strategic/brainstorming question — no single numeric answer.

questions.prompt: How might the organization reduce volatility in raw materials / reduce COGS?
questions.guidance: Possible answers: (1) Long-term supply contracts with feedstock suppliers to lock in pricing; (2) Forward contracts or commodity hedging to reduce feedstock price exposure; (3) Dual-source or multi-source raw material supply to increase negotiating leverage; (4) Vertical integration into feedstock production for the most critical inputs; (5) Pass-through pricing clauses in customer contracts to share feedstock volatility with customers (more feasible for specialty than commodity segments).

math.answer: Strategic/brainstorming question — no single numeric answer.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional changes might an organization facing increased commoditization of product lines consider, and how might it reduce raw material cost volatility?

categories.name: Product/Portfolio Strategy
ideas: Invest in R&D to innovate commodity products into specialty
Exit or divest commodity product lines
Develop a portfolio strategy with major customers (industry-specific sales teams)
Consider outsourcing commodity manufacturing to low-cost producers

categories.name: Organizational Design
ideas: Restructure into Specialty and Commodity BUs by contribution margin
Assign single leaders for each shared service with clear cost-allocation accountability
Negotiate SLAs between shared service leaders and BU leaders
Embed BU-specialized functions into business; retain general services (HR, legal, facilities) in corporate core

categories.name: Customer/Commercial
ideas: Increase partnerships with Specialty chemicals customers for greater volume in high-margin business
Offer a la carte service agreements to commodity customers
Develop industry-specific sales teams that span BUs
Consider preferred-supplier agreements with key Specialty customers

categories.name: Raw Materials / COGS Reduction
ideas: Long-term supply contracts with feedstock suppliers
Commodity hedging / forward contracts on feedstock
Multi-source raw material supply for negotiating leverage
Vertical integration into critical feedstock production
Pass-through pricing clauses in customer contracts for feedstock volatility

recommendation: Reorganize the company into two business units — Specialty and Commodity — based on product line contribution margins (as shown in Exhibit 1)
Specialty BU: continue providing high-level customized service (small batches, custom logistics, technical support, application development)
Commodity BU: adopt a low-cost service model (IT-enabled tools, a la carte service agreements, less favorable terms and conditions to the end customer)

Implement a shared service model where each shared function (logistics, customer service, finance, etc.) has a single leader accountable for costs incurred and responsible for allocating those costs to BUs via negotiated service agreements
risks: Appropriate assignment of product lines to Specialty vs. Commodity BU — and re-assignment over time as products commoditize
Business units do not own manufacturing and supply chain, so those functions remain holders of unallocated cost with little incentive to optimize
Reduced personal service for commodity customers may make the company less competitive and erode top-line revenue and volume
next_steps: Study Manufacturing and Supply Chain to determine which costs can be allocated to BUs where practical
Increase partnerships with Specialty chemicals customers to grow volume in high-margin business
Consider outsourcing or selling one BU to focus resources; or develop a portfolio strategy (e.g., industry-specific sales teams that span BUs) with major customers
